questions.question: From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'until the wheels fall off'.

options.text: To use something until it is destroyed
Play a toy till it is broken
Until it is no longer possible to continue with some activity or pursuit

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Until it is no longer possible to continue with some activity or pursuit**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **'until the wheels fall off'** means to continue doing something for as long as possible, or until it can no longer be done due to exhaustion, failure, or reaching a natural end. (जब तक संभव हो या अंत तक)
 
 
• **Example: **They promised to work on their startup **until the wheels fall off**.
 
 
 
• **'Until it is no longer possible to continue with some activity or pursuit'** correctly defines the idiom, emphasizing the idea of persisting until the very limit of possibility. (जब तक किसी गतिविधि या कार्य को जारी रखना संभव न हो)
 
 
• **Example: **The band decided they would keep touring **until the wheels fall off**.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the meaning of the idiom **'until the wheels fall off'** is to continue an activity until it is no longer possible.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Until it is no longer possible to continue with some activity or pursuit**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **To use something until it is destroyed** (किसी चीज़ का तब तक उपयोग करना जब तक वह नष्ट न हो जाए): This refers to the literal physical destruction of an object through use.
 
 
• **Example:** He used his **hiking boots** until they were completely **destroyed** and unwearable.
 
 
 
• **Play a toy till it is broken** (खिलौने से तब तक खेलना जब तक वह टूट न जाए): A literal action usually associated with children and their toys.
 
 
• **Example:** The toddler **played with the toy** car **till it was broken** into pieces.
 
 
 
• **Do until one is exhausted** (थकने तक काम करना): To work or perform an activity until one has no energy left.
 
 
• **Example:** The athlete continued to **train** until he was **completely exhausted**.

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

hearing the news, Mrs. White fell to the ground.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**on**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The preposition **'on'** (or 'upon'), when followed by a **gerund** (the -ing form of a verb), is used to indicate that an action happens **immediately after** or **as a result of** another event.
 
• In this context, **'on hearing'** means 'as soon as she heard' or 'at the moment she heard' the news.
 
• The sentence describes a **sudden reaction** to an event, which is the standard usage for this prepositional structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *'**On**__ hearing the news, Mrs. White fell to the ground.'*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: 'In'** is generally used to denote **location**, **position**, or **time periods** and does not fit the context of an immediate reaction to a specific event.
 
• **Option 3: 'Under'** usually refers to a **physical position** below something or being **subject to** a condition (e.g., under pressure) and is grammatically incorrect in this phrase.
 
• **Option 4: 'For'** is used to indicate **purpose**, **reason**, or **duration**, which does not convey the intended meaning of a temporal sequence in this sentence.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
Had the technical errors been corrected by the software team before the product launch?

options.text: Did the software team correct the technical errors before the product launch?
Had the software team corrected the technical errors before the product launch?
Has the software team corrected the technical errors before the product launch?
Was the software team correcting the technical errors before the product launch?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Had the software team corrected the technical errors before the product launch?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Passive Voice** and follows the **Past Perfect Tense** in its **Interrogative Form**. The passive structure for this tense is: **Had + Object + been + V3 (Past Participle) + by + Subject?**

• To transform this into the **Active Voice**, the **Agent** of the action (**the software team**) must move to the subject position, and the **Recipient** of the action (**the technical errors**) must move to the object position.

• The **Active Voice** structure for an interrogative sentence in the **Past Perfect Tense** is: **Had + Subject + V3 (Past Participle) + Object?**

• In this conversion, the auxiliary **been** is removed as it is only a marker for the passive construction. The main verb **corrected** remains in its **Past Participle (V3)** form.

• The resulting sentence, **Had the software team corrected the technical errors before the product launch?**, maintains the same **chronological sequence** and **tense consistency** as the original question.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Grammatical Tense Analysis**:

• **Simple Past (Did)**: Used for actions that were completed at a specific time in the past. Using **did** would require the base form of the verb **correct**, which changes the tense of the original query.

• **Present Perfect (Has/Have)**: Connects a past action to the present moment. Using **has** would be grammatically incorrect because the original context is set entirely in the past before a **product launch**.

• **Past Continuous (Was/Were + V-ing)**: Focuses on the duration or ongoing nature of a past action. This changes the **aspect** from a completed action (perfect) to an ongoing one (continuous).

• **Past Perfect Usage**: Specifically used to emphasize that one action was completed before another action or point in the past (the **product launch**).

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
The injured man must be taken to the hospital at once.

options.text: You must be taken the injured man to the hospital at once.
The hospital must take the injured man at once.
Take the injured man to the hospital at once.
Let the injured man be taken to the hospital at once.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Take the injured man to the hospital at once.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The original sentence is in the **Passive Voice**. This is identified by the structure: **Subject (The injured man)** + **Modal Verb (must)** + **be** + **Past Participle (taken)**.

• When a passive sentence expresses an **urgent command**, **advice**, or **instruction** and does not mention a specific **agent** (the doer of the action), it is commonly converted into the **Active Voice** using the **Imperative Mood**.

• An **Imperative Sentence** in the active voice typically begins with the **Base Form of the Verb** (V1). In this case, the verb is **Take**.

• The subject **'you'** is implied in imperative sentences, making it the most suitable active equivalent for a general instruction starting with **'must be'**. Hence, the structure becomes: **Verb (Take)** + **Object (the injured man)** + **Prepositional Phrase (to the hospital at once)**.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Active vs. Passive Voice:**

• **Active Voice:** The subject performs the action (e.g., **'Take the man'**). It is direct and clear.

• **Passive Voice:** The subject receives the action (e.g., **'The man must be taken'**). It is often used when the actor is unknown or less important than the action itself.

• **Analysis of Incorrect Options:**

• **Option 1:** This uses **'must be taken'** which is a **Passive Voice** construction; adding **'You'** as a subject before it creates a grammatical error.

• **Option 2:** This incorrectly identifies the **hospital** as the **agent** (the one doing the taking/carrying), whereas the hospital is actually the **destination**.

• **Option 4:** This uses the **'Let + Object + be + V3'** structure, which is another way to form the **Passive Voice** for imperative sentences. It does not fulfill the requirement for **Active Voice**.

</ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: “No Improvement Required.”
The speaker warned that the economy would hang on a thin thread if corruption continued unchecked.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**hang by a thin thread**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The expression **'hang by a thread'** (or **'hang by a thin thread'**) is a fixed **idiomatic phrase** in English, meaning to be in a very **dangerous**, **uncertain**, or **precarious** situation.
 
• In this idiom, the **preposition 'by'** is mandatory. It indicates the **means** or the **slender connection** by which a person or object is suspended above disaster or failure.
 
• The original sentence used the preposition **'on'**, which is **grammatically incorrect** for this specific figurative expression; idiomatic accuracy requires **'by'** to convey the intended meaning of **instability**.
 
• Using **'hang by a thin thread'** correctly illustrates that the **economy** is at high risk of **collapsing** due to the negative impact of **unchecked corruption**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Etymology and Origin**:
 
 
• This idiom is widely believed to originate from the **legend of Damocles**, where a **king** suspended a **heavy sword** over Damocles' head by a **single horsehair** to demonstrate the **constant peril** faced by those in power.
 
 
 
• **Idiomatic Rigidity**:
 
 
• **Idioms** are **fossilized constructions**. Substituting key elements such as prepositions (e.g., replacing **'by'** with **'upon'** or **'with'**) results in **non-standard English** and is considered a **lexical error** in competitive examinations.
 
 
 
• **Contextual Usage**:
 
 
• The phrase is commonly used in **political science**, **economics**, and **healthcare** to describe systems or patients whose **survival** depends on a very **fragile factor**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Returning from my first morning stroll, I again sallied out upon this special errand. 

A. Wrapping myself in my shaggy jacket of the cloth called bearskin, I fought my way against the stubborn storm. 

B. A muffled silence reigned, only broken at times by the shrieks of the storm. C. Entering, I found a small, scattered congregation of sailors, and sailors’ wives and widows. 

D. The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold, to driving sleet and mist. 

S2. Each silent worshipper seemed purposely sitting apart from the other, as if each silent grief were insular and incommunicable.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph follows a chronological and thematic progression from the start of a journey to the interior of a **chapel**. 
• **Sentence S1** is the introductory sentence where the narrator leaves for a **special errand**. 
• **Sentence D follows S1** as it describes the immediate change in environment: 
• 'The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold, to **driving sleet** and **mist**.' 
• **Sentence A follows D** as it depicts the narrator's physical response to the storm: 
• 'Wrapping myself in my **shaggy jacket** of the cloth called **bearskin**, I fought my way against the **stubborn storm**.' 
• **Sentence C follows A** because it marks the end of the outdoor struggle and the narrator's entry into the destination: 
• '**Entering**, I found a small, scattered **congregation** of **sailors**, and sailors' wives and **widows**.' 
• **Sentence B follows C** as it describes the internal atmosphere of the place the narrator just entered: 
• 'A **muffled silence** reigned, only broken at times by the **shrieks of the storm**.' 
• **Sentence S2 is the concluding sentence**, which provides further detail about the individuals in the **congregation** (worshippers) mentioned in **Sentence C** and the **silence** mentioned in **Sentence B**. 
• The correct sequence is **DACB**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'Returning from my first morning stroll, I again sallied out upon this special errand. The sky had changed from clear, sunny cold, to driving sleet and mist. Wrapping myself in my shaggy jacket of the cloth called bearskin, I fought my way against the stubborn storm. Entering, I found a small, scattered congregation of sailors, and sailors' wives and widows. A muffled silence reigned, only broken at times by the shrieks of the storm. Each silent worshipper seemed purposely sitting apart from the other, as if each silent grief were insular and incommunicable.'</div

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."
It's none uncommon to find street musicians playing in the park during the weekends, drawing crowds from nearby areas.

options.text: nothing uncommon to find street musicians
not uncommon to find street musicians
never uncommon to find streets of musicians

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**not uncommon to find street musicians**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The phrase **'none uncommon'** used in the original sentence is grammatically incorrect because **'none'** is a pronoun or an adverb meaning **'not any'** or **'to no extent'**, and it cannot properly modify the adjective **'uncommon'** in this specific sentence structure.

• The correct expression **'not uncommon'** is a rhetorical device known as **litotes**, where a negative statement (not) is used to affirm a positive sentiment (common); it suggests that the event occurs with reasonable **frequency**.

• In the structure **'It is'** (contracted as **'It's'**), the word **'is'** acts as a **linking verb** which must be followed by an adjective or an **adjectival phrase**; the adverb **'not'** is the standard tool for negating such adjectives in English.

• The term **'street musicians'** is a correctly formed **compound noun** referring to individuals who perform music in public spaces for tips, fitting the context of the sentence perfectly.

 **Additional Information__**

• **'Nothing uncommon'** vs. **'Not uncommon'**:

• **'Nothing'** is a **pronoun**. While one could say **'There is nothing uncommon about this'**, it does not fit the **dummy subject** structure of **'It is...'** as effectively as the adverb **'not'**.

• **'Never uncommon'** and **'Streets of musicians'**:

• **'Never'** is an **adverb of frequency** meaning **'at no time'**; using it here would create an absolute statement that is stylistically unusual for describing a casual weekend observation.

• The phrase **'streets of musicians'** uses a **prepositional phrase** that changes the meaning entirely, suggesting the physical roads are populated by or belong to musicians, rather than describing the **buskers** themselves.

• **Litotes in English**:

• This figure of speech is frequently used in **formal writing** and **literature** to provide **emphasis** through understatement, often making a claim seem more objective or cautious.

</ul

questions.question: Fill in blank (A) with the most suitable adverb.

The correct answer is '**quickly**'. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** __

• The phrase following the blank is '**eager to rehearse her debate speech**'. 
• The word '**eager**' implies a sense of **enthusiasm** or **urgency** to start her preparation. 
• '**Quickly**' is the most appropriate **adverb** as it matches the context of someone who wants to finish a routine task (checking in) rapidly to get to their main goal (rehearsing). 
• Other options like '**calmly**', '**silently**', or '**nervously**' do not directly align with the motivation of being 'eager' to start a task. Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 4**'.
